en.title: Christopher Nolan Links Oppenheimer's Success to His Vision for The Odyssey
en.summary: Christopher Nolan reveals a surprising connection between his historical epic Oppenheimer and his ambitious adaptation of Homer's The Odyssey. The director credits the former's success for paving the way for the latter.
en.body:
Christopher Nolan, a filmmaker renowned for his intricate narratives and grand cinematic scope, has drawn a compelling parallel between his recent blockbuster **Oppenheimer** and his upcoming adaptation of Homer's epic poem, **The Odyssey**. Speaking during a press tour in Beijing, Nolan elaborated on how the critical and commercial triumph of **Oppenheimer** was instrumental in making **The Odyssey** a reality, suggesting a shared philosophical undercurrent binds these seemingly disparate projects.

## A Shared Vision Across Eras

Nolan's adaptation of **The Odyssey** is not merely a literal retelling but a profound exploration of themes that resonate deeply with **Oppenheimer**. Both narratives grapple with the fragility of civilization and the heavy burden of consequences stemming from pivotal historical actions. Nolan highlighted the vast historical distance between the events Homer describes and their transcription, a gap of roughly 400 years. He finds this temporal chasm particularly interesting, noting that Homer was writing about an era his audience perceived as more advanced, a civilization striving to reclaim a glorious past. This concept of cyclical history, of a society at its twilight looking back to a golden age, is a core idea that Nolan sees reflected in the cautionary tale of **Oppenheimer**.

> "The main point is this 400-year-or-so gap between the events that Homer is describing and when Homer’s story was written down or first received by audiences. That’s a pretty interesting gap. For me, I don’t think I’m completely at odds with the way Homer is telling the story when you look at it from a historical perspective. The reason is—and what I became interested in as I adapted it—is that Homer is writing about an era hundreds of years earlier that his audience viewed as being more advanced than theirs. So, while they were a civilization on the rise, they were trying to get back to where they had been 400 years before."

This fascination with the ebb and flow of civilizations, the rise and fall, the echoes of past glories and future regrets, forms a crucial link between **Oppenheimer** and **The Odyssey**. Both protagonists, in their own ways, are left to contend with the profound, often haunting, ramifications of their wartime actions, leaving audiences to ponder the enduring impact of human choices.

## The Impact of Critical Discourse

Beyond the thematic connections, Nolan also touched upon the often-contentious landscape of film criticism. In his interview with political philosophy lecturer Zhong Shu, Nolan expressed thoughts on the perceived flaws within the critical establishment. While the specifics of his critique remain nuanced, it suggests a director who is both engaged with and occasionally frustrated by how films, particularly those dealing with complex historical or philosophical ideas, are dissected and debated. This introspection adds another layer to his approach, indicating a desire for deeper engagement with the material beyond surface-level analysis.

## What's Next

While details regarding the release of Nolan's **The Odyssey** remain under wraps, the success of **Oppenheimer** has undoubtedly emboldened the director to pursue ambitious projects. Fans will be eager to see how Nolan’s signature style and thematic depth translate to the timeless world of Homer's epic.

es.title: Christopher Nolan conecta el éxito de Oppenheimer con su visión para La Odisea
es.summary: Christopher Nolan revela una conexión sorprendente entre su épica histórica Oppenheimer y su ambiciosa adaptación de La Odisea de Homero. El director acredita el éxito de la primera para hacer posible la segunda. La conexión entre estas dos obras parece estar en la exploración de la fragilidad de la civilización y las consecuencias de acciones históricas
es.body:
## Una visión compartida a través de las eras

Christopher Nolan, un cineasta conocido por sus narrativas intrincadas y su gran alcance cinematográfico, ha establecido un paralelo interesante entre su reciente éxito **Oppenheimer** y su próxima adaptación de la épica poesía de Homero, **La Odisea**. Durante una gira de prensa en Beijing, Nolan explicó cómo el éxito crítico y comercial de **Oppenheimer** fue fundamental para hacer posible **La Odisea**, sugiriendo que una corriente filosófica subyacente une estos proyectos aparentemente dispares.

## La conexión entre Oppenheimer y La Odisea

La adaptación de Nolan de **La Odisea** no es solo una narración literal, sino una exploración profunda de temas que resuenan profundamente con **Oppenheimer**. Ambas narrativas luchan con la fragilidad de la civilización y la pesada carga de consecuencias que surgen de acciones históricas clave. Nolan destacó la gran distancia histórica entre los eventos que Homero describe y su transcripción, un lapso de unos 400 años. Encuentra este abismo temporal particularmente interesante, señalando que Homero estaba escribiendo sobre una era que su audiencia consideraba más avanzada, una civilización que intentaba recuperar un pasado glorioso. Este concepto de historia cíclica, de una sociedad en su ocaso que mira hacia atrás a una edad de oro, es una idea central que Nolan ve reflejada en la historia de advertencia de **Oppenheimer**.

> "El punto principal es este lapso de 400 años entre los eventos que Homero describe y cuando la historia de Homero se escribió o se recibió por primera vez por las audiencias. Eso es un abismo temporal bastante interesante. Para mí, no creo que esté completamente en desacuerdo con la forma en que Homero cuenta la historia cuando se considera desde una perspectiva histórica. La razón es - y lo que me interesó al adaptarlo - que Homero está escribiendo sobre una era que ocurrió cientos de años antes, que su audiencia consideraba más avanzada que la suya. Así, mientras eran una civilización en ascenso, estaban tratando de regresar a donde habían estado 400 años antes."

## El impacto del discurso crítico

Más allá de las conexiones temáticas, Nolan también habló sobre el a menudo controvertido panorama de la crítica cinematográfica. En su entrevista con el profesor de filosofía política Zhong Shu, Nolan expresó sus pensamientos sobre las percepciones de los defectos dentro del establecimiento crítico. Si bien los detalles de su crítica siguen siendo matizados, sugiere un director que está comprometido y ocasionalmente frustrado por cómo se analizan y debaten las películas, especialmente aquellas que tratan con ideas históricas o filosóficas complejas. Esta introspección agrega otra capa a su enfoque, indicando un deseo de un compromiso más profundo con el material más allá del análisis de superficie.

## Próximos Pasos

Aunque los detalles sobre el lanzamiento de **La Odisea** de Nolan siguen siendo un misterio, el éxito de **Oppenheimer** ha emboldido sin duda al director para perseguir proyectos ambiciosos. Los fanáticos estarán ansiosos por ver cómo el estilo distintivo de Nolan y su profundidad temática se traducen al mundo intemporal de la épica de Homero.

content_raw: If you have already grown tired of the hundredth interview of The Odyssey team discussing what it was like shooting an entire film on IMAX cameras or capturing everything as practically as possible, then a gift from the gods has now arrived. During the Beijing press stop tour for his box office behemoth, Christopher Nolan sat down with political philosophy lecturer and doctoral student Zhong Shu for the most thorough, fascinating interview yet on the making of his Homer adaptation. For a director who can often be evasive––or perhaps not questioned enough––when it comes to the philosophical decisions behind his movies, Zhong Su does a stellar job in a relatively brief period to get Nolan to open up about his thoughts on “Christianizing” Homer’s poem, the themes of atonement in the film, his thoughts on the flaws of film criticism (be sure to read our less-than-enthused review of his latest), breaking storytelling conventions, his portrayal of the gods, and more. In discussing the adaptation and perspective of historical distance, Nolan says, “The main point is this 400-year-or-so gap between the events that Homer is describing and when Homer’s story was written down or first received by audiences. That’s a pretty interesting gap. For me, I don’t think I’m completely at odds with the way Homer is telling the story when you look at it from a historical perspective. The reason is—and what I became interested in as I adapted it—is that Homer is writing about an era hundreds of years earlier that his audience viewed as being more advanced than theirs. So, while they were a civilization on the rise, they were trying to get back to where they had been 400 years before.” “That idea of a cycle—the idea of, as you say, a civilization at dusk—I think is there in the past, but it’s subtle. When you look at the history, and you see that when they would unearth these walls of old palaces that had crumbled, they called them ‘Cyclopean walls’ because they thought only a giant could have built such grand walls. They had this idea of the greatness of this past civilization. I became interested in that collapse—what they call the ‘catastrophe,’ the Bronze Age collapse—and what happens between the events of the Trojan War and Homer. From a modern perspective, that is something that is frightening, interesting, and intriguing. For me, it partly comes out of having worked on  Oppenheimer  before this, which is very much a film about the end of the world and the collapse of civilization.
